subject: physics
title: I–V characteristics, thermistors and LDRs
key_idea: An I–V graph shows how the current in a component changes with potential difference. A fixed resistor gives a straight line. A filament lamp and a diode do not. Thermistor and LDR resistance falls as temperature or light rises.

sections.heading: I–V graphs of resistors, lamps and diodes

blocks.text: An I–V graph plots current against potential difference for one component. Its shape shows whether the resistance stays constant or changes.

items.meaning: A component where current is directly proportional to potential difference, at constant temperature. Its resistance stays constant.
A component whose I–V graph is curved, so its resistance changes.

diagram.alt: I–V graphs for a fixed resistor, a filament lamp and a diode, with potential difference from negative to positive.

items: The graph is a straight line through the origin, at constant temperature.
Current is directly proportional to potential difference.
The resistance stays constant.
The graph is a curve. The current rises more slowly as the potential difference increases.
The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases.
More current means more collisions between electrons and the ions in the wire. This heats the wire.
Current flows in one direction only.
The diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction, so (almost) no current flows that way.
A light emitting diode (LED) behaves in the same way.
A fixed resistor at constant temperature gives a straight line through the origin.
A filament lamp curves because its resistance increases as it heats up.
A diode passes current in one direction only and has a very high resistance in reverse.

blocks.text: Some components change their resistance with the surroundings. This makes them useful as sensors.

items.meaning: A component whose resistance changes with temperature. In an NTC thermistor, resistance decreases as temperature increases.
A light dependent resistor. Its resistance decreases as light intensity increases.

items: A thermistor is used in circuits such as a thermostat, which controls a heating system.
An LDR is used in circuits such as switching lights on when it gets dark.

sections.heading: Finding an I–V graph by experiment

blocks.text: An I–V graph comes from measuring current and potential difference for one component at a range of settings.

items: Connect an **ammeter** in series with the component.
Connect a **voltmeter** in parallel with the component.
Use a variable resistor, a variable power supply or a different number of cells to change the potential difference.
Reverse the connections to the power supply to get negative values.
Calculate the resistance at each point using the equation below.
To investigate a thermistor, change its temperature and measure the current and potential difference each time. For an LDR, change the light intensity.
Measure current with an ammeter in series and potential difference with a voltmeter in parallel.
Change the potential difference, record pairs of readings and plot current against potential difference.

checks.q: Describe the I–V graph for a fixed resistor at constant temperature.
checks.a: A straight line through the origin. Current is directly proportional to potential difference, so the resistance is constant.

checks.q: Explain why the resistance of a filament lamp increases as the current increases.
checks.a: The filament heats up. More collisions of electrons with the ions in the wire, so the resistance increases.

checks.q: State what happens to the resistance of (a) an NTC thermistor when the temperature increases and (b) an LDR when the light intensity increases.

mistakes.wrong: The ammeter reads 0.0 A because LEDs only allow current in one direction.
mistakes.right: That scores 1 mark only if nothing else is scored. For both marks say the LED has a large resistance in the reverse direction.

mistakes.wrong: A resistor that heats up would still give a straight line.
mistakes.right: A rise in temperature means current and potential difference are no longer directly proportional. The I–V graph is curved because the resistance increases.

mistakes.wrong: The student takes one reading at each potential difference.
mistakes.right: Take repeat readings, calculate a mean and discard any anomalies.

worked_example.question:
Student A investigated how the current in resistor R at constant temperature varied with the potential difference across the resistor.
Student A recorded both positive and negative values of current.

Student B repeated the investigation.
During Student B's investigation the temperature of resistor R increased.

Explain how the increased temperature of resistor R would have affected Student B's results.
answer_points: Current and potential difference would not be directly proportional, so the I–V graph would not be straight (it would be curved).
Because the resistance of R would increase.
worked_example.tip: One mark for the effect on the graph and one for the reason: the resistance increases.

mistakes.wrong: The current in a lamp is directly proportional to the potential difference across it.
mistakes.right: The current increases, but not in equal steps, and doubling the potential difference does not double the current. It is not directly proportional.

mistakes.wrong: The resistance of the lamp changes because it gets hot.
mistakes.right: Link the steps for three marks: resistance increases, the filament heats, there are more collisions of electrons with ions or atoms.

mistakes.wrong: A student quotes data from the table to show that a conclusion is wrong, with no calculation.
mistakes.right: Simply quoting data is ignored. Process it, for example show that doubling the potential difference does not double the resistance.

mistakes.wrong: The resistance of a filament lamp is so high in one direction that no current can pass through.
mistakes.right: That describes a diode. Light emitting diode or LED is also allowed.

mistakes.wrong: The resistance of a thermistor changes as the light intensity changes.
mistakes.right: A thermistor changes with temperature. A light dependent resistor (LDR) changes with light intensity.

mistakes.wrong: A thermistor is used to turn on lights when it gets dark.
mistakes.right: That is an LDR. A thermistor is used in a heating system, because its resistance changes with temperature.

worked_example.question: Explain why the resistance of a filament lamp increases when current increases.
answer_points: More current means more electrons collide with ions in the lattice (or the ions vibrate more).
It is harder for electrons to pass through the lamp.
Which increases the temperature, and therefore the resistance.
worked_example.tip: Any two of the points score. Atoms, particles or molecules are allowed in place of ions.
